Why do we need Current State Journey Mapping?
Current State Journey Mapping is crucial for gaining a deep understanding of how customers and employees currently interact with various facets of the organization. By defining 
customer and employee personas based on their behavior, values, experiences, and expectations, this module helps in pinpointing areas where the current experiences may fall 
short and where targeted improvements can be made. Additionally, a detailed customer journey map serves as a unifying tool that can bring together isolated departments and 
individuals by creating a common language and building shared objectives. This common understanding facilitates a cohesive approach to enhancing the overall customer 
experience and supports the alignment of departmental efforts with overarching transformation goals. Ultimately, Current State Journey Mapping sets the foundation for the 
subsequent modules, such as Customer Journey Pain Points Analysis and Future State Customer & Employee Journeys, by providinga clear and detailed depiction of the current 
interactions that need to be improved to achieve the overall transformation goals.

BEHAVIOURAL
Behavioural segmentation involves 
segmenting customers based on the way they 
interact with a brand. Common variables 
include usage (i.e. purchase frequency), 
exhibited behaviour and habits (i.e. adding 
product to cart but not checking out), and 
product / service preferences. 
This approach can be very granular, e.g. 
tracking customers’ online interactions, and is 
based on proven consumer habits and 
practices. It is particularly helpful for targeting 
marketing interventions to boost conversion. 
However, while consumer behaviour can be 
tracked, it is not always easy to pinpoint the 
motivations behind those behaviours, as they 
can vary greatly from person to person. Also, 
behavioural segmentation is often based on 
complex data constructs that are not always 
easy to understand.
ATTITUDINAL
Attitudinal (or psychographic) segmentation 
takes into account the psychological aspects of 
consumer behaviour by dividing markets 
according to lifestyle, personality traits, values, 
opinions, and interests of consumers. 
This develops a much better understanding of 
the consumer as a human, and helps to 
identify underlying needs and motives. This 
enables more targeted design of services and 
experiences and is best suited to design 
projects. 
However, this approach requires the 
organisation to have detailed insights on the 
consumer through surveying or third party 
data. It also requires robust factor or cluster 
analysis to differentiate and group segments 
appropriately. If an organisation does not 
already have this in place, this segmentation 
approach can be relatively lengthy and costly.

It is possible to take many different approaches to grouping an organisation's customer base. Four of the 
most common methods are described here, each of which have advantages and disadvantages. Each 
project will require a pragmatic approach to selecting the most appropriate segmentation for their design 
problem.
Types of Segmentation
Segmentation and Personas – How to (1/3)
DEMOGRAPHIC
Demographic segmentation sorts a market by 
demographic factors such as age, generation, 
income, family size, gender, occupation, 
nationality, life stage, etc. 
This is one of the simplest methods of 
segmentation as it relies on commonly 
available customer data. Basic demographic 
factors do also have a significant impact on 
customer buying behaviours.
However, similar demographics do not always 
imply similar needs, values or motivations 
within a particular demographic group. 
Therefore, this segmentation approach often 
drives a one-size-fits-all approach that is 
particularly ineffective for design methods.
GEOGRAPHIC
Geographic segmentation involves grouping 
customers by location, country or region.
Like demographic segmentation, this is a very 
simple (but crude) approach to grouping 
customers. It tends to work well in 
cities/countries where there are significant 
differences in socio-economic status in 
different geographic areas, or where there are 
significant changes in lifestyle across regions.
However, it assumes that all consumers in a 
geographic area have similar needs. 
Therefore, geographic segmentation typically 
needs to be used in conjunction with another 
segmentation method to provide useful 
insights for design.

A customer journey map is a visual representation of all 
the interactions a customer has with an organisation. 
These can map the end-to-end journey in detail or focus

consists of a number of ‘layers’, each of which represents 
a specific aspect of the experience, whether it be the 
customer’s expectations, problems they encounter, or 
visual illustrations of each stage of the journey. Journey 
Mapping provides us with an in-depth analysis and

Journey Mapping – Backstage 
Backstage Mapping captures the underlying process 
required in an organisation to deliver the customer and 
user experience.
In order to produce a backstage map, we conduct a 
number of interviews and workshops with the people who 
actually execute the process. We may also extract data 
from other enterprise solutions to provide insight on how 
the journey works including the systems and technology 
used to deliver the customer experience.
In addition to capturing the process, a Backstage Map 
also captures the pain and gain points and the value and 
waste in the journey.
What is Backstage 
Mapping?
Backstage mapping should be used where:
1. A tangible change is required (rather than just a thought 
exercise)
2. The magnitude of financial and speed impact on 
customers is required
When should you do 
Backstage Mapping?
The customer and user experience are delivered 
through the underlying business process, supported by 
technology, and delivered through people. 
As such, a change to the customer experience can 
only be realised by changing the underlying process. 
The Backstage Map provides an understanding of the 
underlying process and a data set from which the 
benefits case can be calculated. 
It is particularly effective in supporting the cost and 
speed benefit calculations.

BEHAVIOURAL
Behavioural segmentation involves 
segmenting customers based on the way they 
interact with a brand. Common variables 
include usage (i.e. purchase frequency), 
exhibited behaviour and habits (i.e. adding 
product to cart but not checking out), and 
product / service preferences. 
This approach can be very granular, e.g. 
tracking customers’ online interactions, and is 
based on proven consumer habits and 
practices. It is particularly helpful for targeting 
marketing interventions to boost conversion. 
However, while consumer behaviour can be 
tracked, it is not always easy to pinpoint the 
motivations behind those behaviours, as they 
can vary greatly from person to person. Also, 
behavioural segmentation is often based on 
complex data constructs that are not always 
easy to understand.
ATTITUDINAL
Attitudinal (or psychographic) segmentation 
takes into account the psychological aspects of 
consumer behaviour by dividing markets 
according to lifestyle, personality traits, values, 
opinions, and interests of consumers. 
This develops a much better understanding of 
the consumer as a human, and helps to 
identify underlying needs and motives. This 
enables more targeted design of services and 
experiences and is best suited to design 
projects. 
However, this approach requires the 
organisation to have detailed insights on the 
consumer through surveying or third party 
data. It also requires robust factor or cluster 
analysis to differentiate and group segments 
appropriately. If an organisation does not 
already have this in place, this segmentation 
approach can be relatively lengthy and costly.

Journey Mapping – Frontstage 
A customer journey map is a visual representation of all 
the interactions a customer has with an organisation. 
These can map the end-to-end journey in detail or focus 
on high-level stages of the journey. A customer journey 
map tells the story of the customer’s experience. It 
consists of a number of ‘layers’, each of which represents 
a specific aspect of the experience, whether it be the 
customer’s expectations, problems they encounter, or 
visual illustrations of each stage of the journey. Journey 
Mapping provides us with an in-depth analysis and 
understanding of the current state customer journeys.
Journey Mapping takes significant time and effort and 
should be used where it will make a real difference to 
transforming Customer Experiences. 
What is journey 
mapping?
Journey Mapping should take place once we have begun to 
acquire some insights into the customers. These insights 
should support the decision about which journeys to map 
and also allow us to build more data rich customer journey 
maps. Journey Mapping can be an activity completed in 
isolation, or to support other aspects of Discovery. For 
example, understanding the current state customer 
journeys can support CX Strategy Development.
When should you do 
journey mapping?
Journey Mapping breaks down a customer’s 
experience into the specific, individual “touchpoints” a 
customer has with an organisation over the course of 
the relationship. Moving through the various 
touchpoints in the customer journey gives the 
organisation a first-person view of every interaction, 
from beginning to end. This brings to life the 
customers’ emotional experience and the pain and 
gain points they encounter along their journey. It also 
helps to flag ‘moments of truth’ – the most i

How to do Journey Mapping?
Journey Mapping: Frontstage – How to
Frame the journey
Journey maps can illustrate either 
existing experiences (current-state 
journey maps) or new experiences that 
are planned but do not yet exist (future-
state journey maps).
Before beginning Journey Mapping, it is 
important to define the specific journey 
or journeys that you will be focusing on 
and the specific customer perspective 
that you will be adopting.
This involves agreeing the boundaries of 
the chosen journey and the personas 
that will be used.
Define the journey phases
Agree the customer journey phases and sub-phases with key 
stakeholders to provide the structure of the map. These represent the 
high-level sections of an experience, such as “inspiration, planning, 
booking, experience, sharing” for a holiday.
These stages define the scale of your visualised experience. The scale 
can range from a high-level journey map that shows the entire end-to-
end experience to a very detailed journey map
showing only a few minutes.
Once these stages have been agreed, decide upon 
the critical layers that add context to your journey. 
These are open-ended and can range from 
channels, emotions, pains, gains to cost 
per touchpoint. 
Capture journey insights

view of the journey. A range of insight gathering
techniques should be used to populate the generic 
touchpoints of the journey – these are the individual 
interactions a customer has with an organization
over the course of the relationship.

Journey Mapping – Backstage 
Backstage Mapping captures the underlying process 
required in an organisation to deliver the customer and 
user experience.
In order to produce a backstage map, we conduct a 
number of interviews and workshops with the people who 
actually execute the process. We may also extract data 
from other enterprise solutions to provide insight on how 
the journey works including the systems and technology 
used to deliver the customer experience.
In addition to capturing the process, a Backstage Map 
also captures the pain and gain points and the value and 
waste in the journey.
What is Backstage 
Mapping?
Backstage mapping should be used where:
1. A tangible change is required (rather than just a thought 
exercise)
2. The magnitude of financial and speed impact on 
customers is required
When should you do 
Backstage Mapping?
The customer and user experience are delivered 
through the underlying business process, supported by 
technology, and delivered through people. 
As such, a change to the customer experience can 
only be realised by changing the underlying process. 
The Backstage Map provides an understanding of the 
underlying process and a data set from which the 
benefits case can be calculated. 
It is particularly effective in supporting the cost and 
speed benefit calculations.
Why is it useful?

Today, retail is no longer transforming through technology, it is fundamentally reinventing
its business model. For decades, competitive advantage was built on product assortment,
pricing, store footprint and operational efficiency. Digital commerce added another channel,
but the objective remained largely unchanged which is facilitate transactions and drive
sales.
That paradigm is rapidly giving way to a far more connected and intelligent model.
Increasingly, retailers are not competing store against store or website against website.
They are competing as ecosystems, bringing together consumers, brands, sellers, logistics
providers, financial institutions, technology partners and increasingly AI-powered services
into integrated platforms, that create value well beyond the point of purchase.
This represents one of the most significant shifts the industry has witnessed in decades.
Retail is moving from being transaction-centric to relationship-centric, from optimising
individual channels to orchestrating interconnected ecosystems, and from generating
revenue solely through commerce to creating multiple engines of value across customer
engagement, data, services and partnerships.
Commerce is becoming an ecosystem business
Previously, retailers created value through a relatively linear model. Products were sourced,
distributed and sold to customers through physical stores or digital channels. Success
depended on improving operational efficiency, optimising inventory and expanding market
reach.
Today's platform businesses operate very differently. Their primary role is not merely to
facilitate transactions but to enable interactions among multiple participants. Consumers,
brands, third-party sellers, logistics providers, payment platforms, financial institutions and
service providers all contribute to creating value for one another.

India has a once-in-a-generation opportunity
India is uniquely positioned to lead this transformation. The convergence of Aadhaar, UPI,
DigiLocker, Account Aggregator has established one of the world's most advanced Digital
Public Infrastructure ecosystems. Combined with affordable connectivity, one of the
youngest digital consumer populations globally and the rapid rise of quick commerce, India
has created conditions where platform-led retail can scale faster than in many developed
markets. Consumers today expect seamless movement between physical stores,
marketplaces, social commerce, mobile applications and emerging AI-powered interfaces.
They increasingly seek integrated experiences that combine discovery, payments, financing,
fulfilment, loyalty and after-sales services into a single journey. For Indian retailers, this
represents a strategic opportunity to evolve from operating individual businesses to
orchestrating interconnected ecosystems capable of delivering continuous value.
The rise of intelligent retail ecosystems
Technology has long enabled retail transformation, but AI is now becoming the operating
system of the modern retail enterprise. Retailers have moved beyond isolated AI use cases
such as recommendation engines or chatbots. To embedding it across merchandising,
demand forecasting, pricing, supply chain planning, customer service and workforce
optimisation. The next phase though of retail evolution will be driven by Agentic AI an
intelligent systems capable of making autonomous decisions, collaborating with other AI
agents and continuously learning from every interaction. Commerce will increasingly
become a collaboration between intelligent systems rather than a sequence of isolated
human decisions.
